# Incident Report — 2026-02-28-traffic-analysis-exercise.pcap

## Victim Host
- **IPv4:** 10.2.28.88
- **MAC:** 00:19:d1:b2:4d:ad
- **Windows hostname:** DESKTOP-TEYQ2NR (confirmed via DHCP option 12 and NBNS `<00>`/`<20>` records)
- **Logged-in user:** `brolf` (Kerberos AS-REQ CNameString, domain EASYAS123, DC at 10.2.28.2 / easyas123-dc.easyas123.tech)
- Note: a second, unrelated host (`brads-MBP`, MAC 00:e0:4c:68:08:00) briefly appears in DHCP broadcast traffic — different device, not implicated.

## Malware Family
**NetSupport RAT** (legitimate NetSupport Manager remote-control software abused as a commodity RAT). **Signature-confirmed**, based on:
- HTTP `User-Agent: NetSupport Manager/1.3` on every beacon
- The exact NetSupport client protocol markers observed in the raw HTTP bodies: `CMD=POLL\nINFO=1\nACK=1` (client poll) and `CMD=ENCD\nES=1\nDATA=<encrypted blob>` (encoded C2 exchange) — this is the documented NetSupport client-to-gateway wire format
- The well-known `POST /fakeurl.htm` decoy URI NetSupport RAT uses to disguise its C2 channel as ordinary web traffic

## Infection Timeline (from capture)
1. **t=44.44s** — DESKTOP-TEYQ2NR resolves `www.fmcsa.dot.gov` → 23.64.147.24 and opens a TLS session (content unobservable — encrypted; likely the lure/decoy page or a tab open at the time of compromise; no direct malicious content confirmed from this connection).
2. **t=44.77s** — DNS query for `vadusa.xyz` resolves to **45.131.214.85**.
3. **t=45.05s** — First `POST http://45.131.214.85/fakeurl.htm` fires (single persistent TCP connection, source port 51912 → dest port 443, tcp.stream 40).
4. From there, the infected host beacons every **~60 seconds** for the remainder of the capture (264 POSTs observed, spanning ~4.3 hours from 45.0s to 15682.0s relative time), all on the one long-lived TCP stream.
5. No executable payload transfer is visible in this capture — delivery of the RAT client itself happened either before the capture window or via the encrypted `fmcsa.dot.gov` TLS session, so no dropped file name or hash can be grounded in the traffic.

## Indicators of Compromise

| Type | Value | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| C2 endpoint | `45.131.214.85:443` | Sole destination of tcp.stream 40; 264 HTTP POSTs over ~4.3 hrs, frames 2638–15499 |
| Domain | `vadusa.xyz` | DNS query (frame 1559/1747) resolved by DC (10.2.28.2) to 45.131.214.85 at frame 2566 |
| URL | `http://45.131.214.85/fakeurl.htm` | HTTP request line on every beacon frame (e.g. frame 2638) |
| C2 protocol marker | `CMD=POLL` / `CMD=ENCD` NetSupport wire format | Raw bytes in HTTP response/request bodies on tcp.stream 40 |
| HTTP User-Agent | `NetSupport Manager/1.3` | Present on all 264 POST requests to 45.131.214.85 |

No file names or SHA256 hashes could be grounded — no binary object was transferred over any protocol captured in this pcap.

## Benign Context (ruled out, not IOCs)
Standard Windows/AD/Office/Edge background noise sharing the same host: `ctldl.windowsupdate.com`, `ocsp.digicert.com`, `msedge.b.tlu.dl.delivery.mp.microsoft.com` (BITS component downloads), `login.microsoftonline.com`, `*.events.data.microsoft.com`, `www.msftconnecttest.com` (NCSI), `www.bing.com`/`www.msn.com`/`assets.msn.com`, `officeclient.microsoft.com`/`odc.officeapps.live.com`, `config.edge.skype.com`, `acroipm2.adobe.com`/`armmf.adobe.com` (Adobe ARM), `services.gfe.nvidia.com`, `update.googleapis.com`, `deff.nelreports.net`, `oneclient.sfx.ms`. Domain SMB/LDAP/Kerberos/DCERPC (samr, lsarpc, drsuapi) traffic between 10.2.28.88 and the DC (10.2.28.2) is normal Group Policy / domain-membership chatter.

## Summary
DESKTOP-TEYQ2NR (10.2.28.88, MAC 00:19:d1:b2:4d:ad), logged in as domain user `brolf` on the EASYAS123 AD domain, was infected with **NetSupport RAT**. Within a second of a DNS lookup for `www.fmcsa.dot.gov` (a likely lure/decoy tab), the host resolved the attacker domain `vadusa.xyz` to 45.131.214.85 and immediately began a persistent, ~60-second-interval C2 beacon disguised as HTTP traffic to `/fakeurl.htm`, continuing for the full 4.3-hour remainder of the capture. No dropped executable or file hash is present in this pcap, so the initial delivery mechanism could not be recovered from the traffic alone.
